title: GPU scheduling and sharing on Kubernetes
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: The NVIDIA device plugin advertises `nvidia.com/gpu` as an extended resource.
Time slicing lets several pods share a GPU in turns with no memory isolation, which suits light inference and development.
Taint GPU nodes so that only pods that tolerate the taint land on them, and use node selectors or affinity for a card type.
A distributed training job needs all its workers at once.
Export DCGM metrics for GPU utilisation, memory and power.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: GPUs allocated and idle
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Eight GPUs were reserved for a notebook and used less than five percent for a week.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl exec dcgm-exporter-x -- curl -s localhost:9400/metrics | grep DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL | head -2
The notebook held its GPUs between experiments.
The team moved light work to time sliced GPUs, added an idle culler that releases notebooks after two hours and published per team utilisation so owners could see the waste.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Giving whole GPUs to light workloads.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Vector databases and retrieval operations
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: An embedding model turns text into a vector of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers.
A flat index compares the query to every vector and is exact but slow at scale.
A vector of 1536 floats takes about six kilobytes, so ten million vectors need roughly sixty gigabytes before the index overhead.
Most queries filter by metadata, such as tenant or date.
Recall is the share of the true nearest neighbours that the index returns.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Search quality dropped after an embedding upgrade
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Retrieval started returning unrelated documents after a model version change.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -c "select count(*) from docs where embed_model = 'v2'"
New documents were embedded with the new model while old ones kept the old vectors, so queries compared vectors from different spaces.
The team re-embedded the whole collection into a new index, switched over at once and stored the model version with every vector to catch this in future.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Mixing vectors from different models in one index.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: RAG pipelines in production
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Documents are ingested, split into chunks, embedded and indexed.
Chunks that are too small lose context and chunks that are too large dilute the match and use prompt space.
Combine vector search with keyword search, since exact names and error codes are matched better by keywords.
Tell the model to answer only from the supplied text and to say when the answer is not there.
Track document versions and re-index changes on a schedule or by event.

title: Failure and recovery: A confident answer from a deleted policy
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
The assistant quoted a policy that had been withdrawn a month earlier.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -c "select doc_id, updated_at, deleted from chunks where doc_id = 'policy-17' limit 2"
The source system marked the document deleted, but the index never received the delete event.
The ingestion job was changed to process deletes, a nightly reconciliation compares the index with the source and answers now show the document date.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No handling of deleted or updated documents.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: LLM gateways: routing, caching and rate limits
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A gateway exposes one API to applications and forwards to providers or self hosted models.
Route simple requests to cheaper, faster models and hard ones to stronger models.
An exact cache returns a stored answer for an identical request, which is safe for deterministic calls.
Limit requests and tokens per minute per team and per key, and set monthly budgets with alerts.
Never give provider keys to applications.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A retry storm during a provider outage
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
When a provider slowed down, retries from every service tripled the load and the gateway fell over.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s localhost:4000/metrics | grep -E 'requests_total|retries_total' | head -3
Each client retried three times and the gateway retried again, multiplying traffic.
A shared retry budget, exponential backoff with jitter, a circuit breaker that failed fast to the fallback provider and per team limits stopped the next incident from spreading.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Provider keys inside applications.

title: LLM observability, evaluation and guardrails
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Record each step as a span: retrieval, prompt, model call and tool calls.
Build a test set of real questions with expected answers or checks.
Track thumbs up and down, retries, answer abandonment and escalations to humans.
Check inputs for prompt injection and sensitive data, and outputs for policy violations, personal data and format errors.
Providers update models, documents change and users ask new things.

title: Failure and recovery: A silent change after a model update
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
The provider updated a model alias and answers became longer and costlier overnight.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=avg(llm_output_tokens)' | head -c 140
The application used a moving alias, so behaviour changed without a deploy.
The team pinned an explicit model version, added an alert on average output length and cost per request and scheduled a nightly run of the evaluation set.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Watching only latency and errors.

title: Cost and capacity engineering for inference
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: API prices are quoted per million input and output tokens.
Throughput is measured in tokens per second per GPU, and it depends on the model size, precision, batch size and context length.
Continuous batching serves many requests together and raises utilisation.
GPU nodes take minutes to start and models take more minutes to load, so reactive scaling is slow.
Hosted APIs have no fixed cost and no operations, and suit low or spiky traffic.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A self hosted model that cost more than the API
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A team bought GPUs to save money and found the cost per token was three times higher.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=avg(DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL)' | head -c 150
Two GPUs at about three dollars an hour served 980 million tokens a month at fifteen percent utilisation, which cost more per million tokens than the hosted price.
The team moved light traffic to the API, kept the GPUs for steady high volume jobs and raised utilisation with batching before buying more.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Benchmarking with unrealistic prompts.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
